Connect a supported spectrometer with a data-capable OTG cable (micro-USB to USB-C for micro-USB units). The app opens automatically when it is plugged in. To try the app without hardware, turn on the simulator in Setup.
no fire detection (needs a NIR unit covering 766–770 nm)
Plug a supported spectrometer into the phone\'s USB-C port with a data-capable OTG cable (micro-USB units need a micro-USB to USB-C OTG cable), or turn on the simulator in Setup.

PocketSpectro turns an Android phone into a portable console for Ocean Optics USB spectrometers, connected directly to the phone\'s USB-C port. It controls the spectrometer, shows live spectra in counts, absorbance or transmittance/reflectance with dark, reference, averaging, smoothing and nonlinearity correction, and logs GPS-tagged spectra for later analysis. With a near-infrared spectrometer that covers 766–770 nm, a fire-detection mode watches for the potassium emission doublet that burning vegetation produces, with an audible alarm and a map of detections, for hand-held or vehicle-based surveys.

RFSAT Limited is a non-profit research and development SME based in Dublin, Ireland, with a research office in Athens, Greece. It carries out applied research and technology development under national and EU funding programmes, including Horizon Europe, spanning digital signal processing, micro-embedded sensing, autonomous systems, GNSS positioning, and environmental and e-Health monitoring.
USB protocols ported from Ocean Optics SeaBreeze (MIT)
Any Ocean Optics / Ocean Insight USB spectrometer is recognised when plugged in. Status in this version:
Experimental: driver ported from Ocean\'s SeaBreeze sources, not yet tested on that hardware. Needs external power: also needs a powered USB hub or the unit\'s own supply.
Not affiliated with or endorsed by Ocean Optics / Ocean Insight.
No spectrum yet. Press Run or Single.
Dark: block the light path (or use the built-in shutter), then store. Reference: point at the white/blank standard. Absorbance and %T/%R need both, taken at the current integration time.

Pi rule active: the K I lines are compared with the mean of the whole spectrum, so a bright continuum near 766 nm can be reported as fire with no emission lines present. Use Recommended for detection.
This spectrometer\'s range (%1$s–%2$s nm) does not cover the K I lines at 766–770 nm; fire detection is not meaningful.
Recommended: 200 ms, K I lines by wavelength, each line against the local continuum, 10 % threshold.

Pi preset: exactly as the Pi ran it: one raw 200 ms scan (its daemon ignored the requested boxcar 3), pixel windows 278–282 / 287–291, lines against the whole-spectrum mean. For comparing with old data.
Not logging. Settings below apply to the next session.
Interval 0 saves every spectrum; max 0 means no limit.
One CSV per session (one row per spectrum)

Each session gets its own folder with spectra.csv (or one text file per spectrum), fire.csv with the K-line analysis of every saved spectrum, detections.kml (track and confirmed detections, opens in Google Earth) and session.txt with the device calibration and settings. Logged counts are the processed counts shown on the Live screen (dark, nonlinearity and boxcar as flagged per row).

Simulated near-infrared spectrometer for trying the app without hardware
Adds water / C-H absorption bands, for trying absorbance and %T
Uses the unit\'s stored coefficients; applied once a dark is stored
Gradient indices as on the Pi; the candidate peak is the next pixel.
Off matches the Pi (raw counts). The 10 % threshold was tuned on raw counts.
No detections yet. Confirmed fire detections with a GPS fix appear here as red markers, and logged sessions draw their survey track in blue.
No spectrum was saved with this detection.
Experimental (driver ported, not yet tested on hardware)
Experimental; needs its own power supply or a powered USB hub
Shutter not available on this unit: block the light path for darks
Take a dark before the reference
Reference stored, but it is SATURATED: shorten integration

Simulator only. Adds K I emission (766.5 / 769.9 nm) to the simulated spectrum so the detector, alarm, journal and map can be tried without a fire. Detections from simulated incidents are recorded like real ones and marked as simulated; clear them in Log → Sessions.
Strength 1 gives about 27 % above the continuum at 200 ms; around 0.35 sits at the default 10 % threshold, for testing borderline cases.
Incidents start at random (on average once per interval), each with its duration and strength varied by ±50 %. They ramp up and down over about 1.5 s.

Each tool turns the spectrometer into an instrument for one job. A tool is greyed out when the connected spectrometer does not cover the wavelengths it needs. With the simulator, every tool can be tried before buying a spectrometer.
No spectrometer connected. Every tool can be tried with the built-in simulator.
Simulated spectrometer (its range decides which tools apply):
This tool needs a spectrometer covering %1$s–%2$s nm; the connected one covers %3$s–%4$s nm.
With the simulator, pick another simulated model on the Tools list (for example STS-VIS for colour work).
Potassium (K I) flame emission at 766/770 nm, with alarm and a map of detections.
Tracks chosen emission lines (flame tests, lamps, lasers): wavelength, strength and width, with an optional alarm.
NDVI, red-edge position and water index of leaves or canopy; a GPS survey drawn on the map.
Identifies a sample by comparing its spectrum with a library you build: genuine or fake, material sorting.
Beer–Lambert: calibrate with standards, then read the concentration of an unknown sample.
CIE L*a*b* colour and ΔE₀₀ against a stored standard, for quality control and ripeness.
Peak, width, chromaticity and colour temperature of LEDs and lamps; lux and PAR with a reference meter.
One value against time: reaction rates, drying, fading; first-order rate fit and CSV export.
Needs: a near-infrared unit (STS-NIR, ST-NIR). No accessories.
Needs: any unit, with the input or a fibre pointed at the source.
Needs: a unit covering red and near-infrared (660–800 nm), a white reference panel, daylight or a lamp.
Needs: any unit, a reflection probe or lamp, and a white tile for reflectance.
Needs: any unit, a cuvette holder, a light source and standards.
Needs: a visible-range unit (380–780 nm), a white tile and a lamp or reflection probe.
Needs: any unit; colour figures need the visible range. A lamp of known temperature corrects the response.
Needs: any unit; a cuvette holder and light source for absorbance.
Records this result with the GPS position.
Store a dark, then point the probe at the white reference tile or panel under the same light. Reflectance = sample / white.
Store a dark, then measure the blank (cuvette with solvent only). Absorbance = −log10(sample / blank).
Store a dark (shutter closed or input covered) so the counts are the true signal.
Simulator only: choose what the simulated probe looks at. While a white reference or blank is stored, the simulator shows the white tile or blank cuvette by itself.
Choose the halogen lamp and tap “Use as lamp” above to calibrate the response, then switch to an LED.
Simulated cuvette with a blue dye (absorption peak 664 nm). Pick a concentration for the standards, or an unknown sample.
Starts a simulated bleaching reaction in the cuvette: the dye fades with first-order rate k.
None of these lines is inside this spectrometer\'s range.

Each line is measured above a straight continuum through flanks 3–9 nm either side. A line counts as present when it is above the threshold and the signal-to-noise minimum. With the alarm on, a new line sounds the alarm and is put on the map.
Store a dark and a white reference (Dark and reference, below) to see the indices.

NDVI above about 0.6 means dense green cover; stress lowers NDVI and moves the red edge to shorter wavelengths. The water index (900/970 nm) falls as leaves dry. Indices are shown only where the spectrometer covers their bands.
Records NDVI with the GPS position at the set interval while you walk or drive; the points appear on the Map, coloured from brown (bare) to green (dense).
Library empty: add reference spectra below

The score is how much of the measured spectrum the library spectrum explains after scaling it (brightness does not matter); 100 % is identical. Build the library from known-good samples measured the same way.
No white reference stored: saving raw counts, which also include the lamp and detector. Reflectance is more robust.
Tip: store a white reference so samples are compared as reflectance.
Store a dark and a blank (Dark and reference, below) to measure absorbance.
Outside the range of the standards: the result is an extrapolation.
Put each standard in the holder, enter its concentration and tap Add standard. Two or more give a calibration line (A = slope × c + intercept).
Add at least two standards of different concentration.
Store a dark and a white reference (Dark and reference, below) to measure colour.
No standard stored. Measure the reference sample and tap Set as standard.
ΔE₀₀: below 1 not visible, 1–2 close, 2–5 noticeable, above 5 clearly different.
Uncorrected: includes the detector\'s own spectral response, so colour figures are approximate. Calibrate with a lamp below.
Point the input at a halogen lamp of known colour temperature (for example 2856 K, CIE illuminant A) and tap Use as lamp: the detector response is then divided out of every measurement.
For absolute values, put a lux meter next to the input, enter its reading and tap Set scale (needs the lamp calibration and a cosine corrector).
Time (s) since the start of recording; dashed: first-order fit
First-order fit: value = v₀·e^(−kt). Record at a fixed wavelength; the CSV export keeps every point.

plurals.item: %1$d result with GPS position (vegetation survey, matches, concentrations…), shown on the Map tab
%1$d results with GPS position (vegetation survey, matches, concentrations…), shown on the Map tab

resources.string: Keeps the continuum flank below the atmospheric O2 A band, which in daylight sits next to the K I lines. Recommended outdoors.
Partial: this unit covers %1$s–%2$s nm of the %3$s–%4$s nm needed
Part of the visible range only

This spectrometer covers %1$s–%2$s nm of the visible range (380–780 nm), about %3$s %% of what the eye responds to. Only colours that differ there can be detected and monitored: %4$s. Outside the range the reflectance is taken as the nearest measured value, so L*a*b* values are approximate; compare only with a standard measured on this spectrometer.
Watches for the potassium emission doublet (K I 766.5 and 769.9 nm) that burning vegetation gives off, and raises an alarm when a fire is confirmed.

1. Point the spectrometer input at the area to watch; no accessories are needed.
2. Tap Monitoring ON. The banner is green (no fire), amber (signal being confirmed) or red (fire detected).
3. With Alarm ON, a confirmed detection sounds and vibrates.
4. Each confirmed detection with a GPS fix is saved and shown on the Map as a flame; tap it for the spectrum and details.

Use the Recommended preset; the Pi preset only reproduces the old Raspberry Pi rule for comparison with earlier data. Threshold, confirmation frames and the oxygen-band option are in Setup. With the simulator, test it with Simulated fire incidents.
Measures chosen emission lines: their exact wavelength and shift, their width, and how far they rise above the local background.

1. Point the input at the source: flame, lamp, laser or plasma.
2. Choose a line set: Flame tests, Hg-Ar lamp, Lasers, or Custom (for example "Na 589.3, H 656.3").
3. Read the table: ● marks lines present above the threshold and the signal-to-noise minimum.
4. Line alarm ON sounds when a new line appears and saves it on the map.

Shorten the integration time if the strongest line saturates. Each line is measured against its own background, so a bright continuum does not fake a line. The Hg-Ar set is also a quick check of the wavelength calibration.
Computes vegetation indices from the reflectance of leaves or canopy: NDVI (green cover), red-edge position (chlorophyll and stress), chlorophyll and water indices.

1. In Dark and reference, tap Dark + white reference while the probe looks at a white reference panel under the same light (daylight or a lamp).\n2. Point at the plants: NDVI and the indices update live.\n3. For a survey, set the interval and tap Survey ON, then walk or drive; the points appear on the Map from brown (bare) to green (dense).
Take a new white reference when the light changes (clouds, sun angle). NDVI above about 0.6 means dense healthy cover; stress lowers NDVI and moves the red edge to shorter wavelengths.
Identifies a sample by comparing its spectrum with a library of reference spectra you record yourself: genuine or fake, material sorting, batch checks.

1. Store a dark and a white reference (white tile, same lamp and probe), so samples are compared as reflectance.
2. Build the library: measure each known sample, type its name and tap Add to library.
3. Measure an unknown: the best match and its score are shown; below the threshold the result is No match.
4. Save to map records the result with its GPS position.
Measure library samples and unknowns the same way (distance, angle, lamp). Spectral shape matters, brightness does not. With the simulator, Add demo library loads five materials to try.
Measures the concentration of a substance in solution from its absorbance (Beer–Lambert law), using a calibration made with standards.

1. Put a cuvette with solvent only (the blank) in the holder and tap Dark + blank.
2. Insert a standard, set the wavelength (or tap Use peak), enter its concentration and tap Add standard; repeat for at least two, better four or five, standards.
3. Insert the unknown: its concentration is shown, in green when inside the range of the standards.
4. Save to map records it with the sample name.
Keep absorbance between about 0.1 and 1; dilute stronger samples. Use the same cuvette in the same orientation. An R² close to 1.000 means a good calibration.
Measures colour like a colorimeter (CIE L*a*b*, illuminant D65, 2° observer) and the colour difference ΔE₀₀ from a stored standard, for quality control or ripeness.

1. Store a dark and a white reference with the probe on a white tile.
2. Measure the reference sample and tap Set as standard.
3. Measure samples: ΔE₀₀ and PASS or FAIL against the tolerance are shown.
4. Save to map records the results with their GPS position.

Full colour needs 380–780 nm; with a unit covering only part of it (such as the STS-NIR) only differences in the covered part are seen. Keep the same lamp and geometry. ΔE₀₀ below 1 is invisible, above 5 clearly different.

Characterises light sources such as LEDs, lamps and lasers: peak wavelength, width and centroid; with a visible-range unit also chromaticity and colour temperature; after scaling to a lux meter, illuminance and plant-growth light (PPFD).

1. Cover the input and tap Dark (shutter).
2. Point the input, ideally with a cosine corrector or diffuser, at the source; shorten the integration time if it saturates.
3. For accurate colour, point at a halogen lamp of known temperature (for example 2856 K) and tap Use as lamp; the detector response is corrected from then on.
4. For lux and PPFD, enter a lux meter reading taken at the same place and tap Set scale.
Without the lamp calibration, colour figures include the detector\'s own response and are approximate.
Follows one value over time (absorbance, the reflectance or transmittance ratio, or raw counts at a chosen wavelength) for reaction rates, drying, fading or stability tests.

1. For absorbance or ratio, store a dark and a blank (cuvette with solvent).
2. Choose the quantity and the wavelength.
3. Start the process and tap Recording ON; the graph grows and the first-order fit gives the rate constant k and the half-life.
4. Share CSV exports every point.
Use the wavelength of the absorption peak for the strongest signal. A first-order fit (R² near 1) suits fading and bleaching; for other processes use the initial rate.
Haze (aerosol optical depth) and water vapour in the air from the direct sun, like an AERONET photometer.
Needs: a unit covering 440–1020 nm (STS-NIR or STS-VIS), a narrow collimator tube and a neutral-density filter.
Sunburn-weighted solar UV and the UV index, with the UV-B share.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV, 290–400 nm), a cosine corrector and a reference UV index once for the scale.
Recognises street and indoor lamps (sodium, mercury, metal halide, fluorescent, LED, halogen) and maps them for light-pollution surveys.
Needs: a visible unit (STS-VIS, or STS-UV up to 640 nm); a diffuser helps.
Sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence in the oxygen bands: plant stress before it shows in NDVI.
Needs: a near-infrared unit (STS-NIR), a white reference panel and direct sunlight.
Nitrate from the 220 nm band and organic matter from UV254 (with SUVA), in a quartz cuvette.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV), a deuterium–halogen lamp, a cuvette holder and a 10 mm quartz cuvette.
Your own calibration (PLS): sugar, dry matter, moisture… from samples with known values.
Needs: any unit (NIR is best for food and agriculture), a white reference, and samples measured by a reference method.
Identifies plastics, minerals, solvents and medicines from their Raman bands.
Needs: STS-NIR, a 785 nm laser (≥100 mW, eye protection!), a long-pass filter and a probe.
EU UV indices K232, K268 and ΔK: extra virgin, virgin, or above the virgin limits.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV), a deuterium lamp, quartz cuvettes and iso-octane.
Beer colour (EBC and SRM), wine colour intensity and hue, honey Pfund grade.
Needs: a visible unit (STS-VIS), a cuvette holder with a white lamp and cuvettes.
Temperature of glowing objects (kilns, embers, molten metal, filaments) from the shape of their light.
Needs: any unit (NIR is best below 1500 K) and one calibration with a halogen lamp of known temperature.
Thickness of transparent films and coatings (0.5–50 µm) from their interference fringes.
Needs: any unit, a reflection probe with a lamp and a white reference.
Transmittance of filters, sunglasses and safety glasses: category, UV400, blue-light, cut-on, optical density.
Needs: any unit with a lamp across the beam (UV unit for the UV checks).
Self-test of the spectrometer: dark noise, hot pixels, linearity and wavelength accuracy, with a report.
Needs: a steady lamp, and a mercury-argon lamp for the wavelength check.
Store a dark, then the open beam (nothing in the holder). Transmittance = sample / open beam.
Simulated sky: AOD %1$s at 500 nm, α %2$s, water vapour %3$s cm.
A calibrated UV meter would read %1$s.
Store a dark first (Dark and reference, below).
Saturated: shorten the integration time or use a stronger ND filter.
The sun is too low (below 5°) for reliable values.
Not calibrated yet: see Calibration below (known values or a Langley plot).
AOD is the haze of the air column: 0.05 is very clean, above 0.5 hazy, smoky or dusty. α near 0 means coarse dust, near 2 fine smoke or pollution.
Hours since the first point; one point every 30 s.

The photometer needs the signal the sun would give above the atmosphere (V₀) for each channel. Set it from known values (a nearby AERONET station or a calibrated photometer at the same time), or by a Langley plot.
On a clear, stable morning or afternoon, record while the sun moves from low (airmass 6) to higher (airmass 2), then fit. Mountain sites work best.
Store a dark first (Dark and reference, below).
Not scaled yet: enter a reference UV index once (Scale, below).
Dashed: sunburn (erythemal) weighting, scaled to the spectrum.

Counts become a UV index with one factor: measure at the same time and place as a calibrated UV meter or a nearby official station and enter its value. Keep the same cosine corrector and fibre afterwards.
broad sodium band with a dip at 589 nm
Colour temperature and blue share are approximate until the detector response is calibrated (Light tool, Use as lamp).
Drive or walk past street lights with the input pointing at them; each recognised lamp is saved with its position at the interval, coloured by type on the Map.
Shown while a fire is detected.
Sunlight-like spectrum: probably a glint, not a flame.
Store a dark and a white reference under the same sunlight first (below).
The oxygen band is shallow: this needs direct sunlight, not lamps or deep shade.

Values are % of the incoming sunlight near the band. Healthy, actively photosynthesising leaves glow more (about 1–2 % at 760 nm); stressed ones less. Compare plants measured the same way; the absolute value is biased low at this resolution.
Nitrate absorbs below 240 nm; organic matter absorbs across the UV, so it is subtracted using 2 × A275 (Standard Methods 4500-NO₃⁻ B). The EU drinking-water limit is 50 mg/L nitrate (11.3 mg/L as N).
Nitrate response: %1$s absorbance per mg/L N at 220 nm (10 mm). Measure a nitrate standard and enter its value to calibrate.
Calibrate the detector response with a lamp of known temperature first (below).
Dashed: Planck curve at the fitted temperature.
Fits Planck\'s law to the shape of the light, so the emissivity of a grey body cancels. Glass, flames with strong lines or non-grey surfaces add error; narrow the range to skip lines.
Point at a halogen lamp of known colour temperature (for example 2856 K) and tap Use as lamp. The Light tool shares this calibration.
Store a dark and a white reference first (below).
Dashed: thin-film model at the fitted thickness.
Refractive index of the film: about 1.5 for lacquers and polymers, 1.46 silica, 2.0 silicon nitride
Thickness scales with 1/n, so a wrong index gives a proportionally wrong result. With an unknown substrate only the fringe spacing is used (needs at least 1.5 fringes).
Store a dark and the open beam first (below).

Categories per ISO 12312-1: 0 = 80–100 %, 1 = 43–80 %, 2 = 18–43 %, 3 = 8–18 %, 4 = 3–8 % (not for driving). UV400 means at most 1 % of UV passes up to 400 nm. Optical density is limited by the dynamic range: \"≥\" marks a lower bound.
Store a dark and a white reference first (below): models use reflectance.
No models yet: create one below, or build the demo model with the simulator.
This model needs %1$s–%2$s nm, which this spectrometer does not cover.
needs 5 or more samples with different values
Dots: model against the reference values of the samples; dashed: perfect agreement.

Add 20–50 samples covering the whole range you expect, measured the same way (same probe, distance and light), each with its value from a reference method. The error tells how far a prediction may be off.
This unit does not cover the Raman range for a %1$s nm laser (shifts 250–3400 cm⁻¹).
Raman shift (cm⁻¹), fluorescence background removed; markers: bands of the best match.
The exact laser wavelength sets the shift scale: if some laser light leaks through the filter, use its measured position. Raman light is weak: use 1–10 s integration and average several scans.
%1$d common materials are built in. Add your own references: measure a known sample and add its peaks.
Store a dark and the blank (iso-octane in the same cuvette) first (below).

Dissolve 0.25 g of oil in 25 mL iso-octane (1 g per 100 mL) and measure in a 10 mm quartz cuvette against iso-octane. Dilute more if the absorbance at 232 nm is above about 1.5, and enter the concentration used.

Limits of Regulation (EEC) No 2568/91 as amended: extra virgin K232 ≤ 2.50, K268 ≤ 0.22, |ΔK| ≤ 0.01; virgin ≤ 2.60, ≤ 0.25, ≤ 0.01. High K232 means oxidation (dienes); high K268 and ΔK mean ageing or refined oil. These UV indices are only part of the official grading (acidity, peroxide value and a tasting panel are also needed).
turbid: filter or degas, the colour reads high
OIV method, reported for a 10 mm path: measure red wines in a 1 mm cell (enter the path). Young reds have a hue near 0.5–0.7; it rises towards 1 and above as wine ages and browns.
50 % honey solution (w/v) in water against water, 10 mm path; mm Pfund = −38.70 + 371.39 × A635 (USDA colour classes).
Test running: keep the input as described until it finishes.
The test did not complete (no frames, or no Hg-Ar lines found).
Closes the shutter where the unit has one; otherwise cover the input with its cap first. Takes 10 single scans at the current integration time.
Point at a steady lamp (signal at about half scale at the current integration time). The test measures at ¼, ½ and the full integration time: counts per millisecond should stay the same.
Point at a mercury-argon calibration lamp (for example an Ocean HG-2) and check: the measured lines should be within 0.5 nm of their true positions.

Measures how hazy the air is (aerosol optical depth, AOD) and how much water vapour it holds, by looking straight at the sun through a narrow tube, the way AERONET sun photometers do. Readings can be put on the map, for example for air-quality and ENACT-style surveys.

1. Fit the spectrometer input with a narrow collimator tube (2–5° field of view) and a neutral-density filter, on a tripod.
2. Store a dark with the input covered (Dark and reference).
3. Aim the tube exactly at the sun: the signal is highest when it is centred. Shorten the integration time if it saturates.
4. Calibrate once: enter AOD, α and water vapour from a nearby AERONET station measured at the same time, or record a Langley plot on a clear morning.
5. Read AOD at 500 nm, the Ångström exponent and the water vapour; Save to map stores them with your position.

Only measure when no cloud is near the sun. The calibration stays valid while the tube, filter and fibre stay the same; repeat it every few months. AOD below 0.1 is clean air; smoke and dust easily exceed 0.5.
Measures solar UV and weights it by the skin\'s sunburn sensitivity (the CIE erythemal curve) to give the UV index, with the share coming from UV-B.

1. Fit a cosine corrector on the input and point it straight up, with a free view of the sky.
2. Store a dark with the input covered.
3. Once: next to a calibrated UV meter, or at the time and place of an official UV measurement, enter its UV index and tap Set scale.
4. Read the UV index and the risk level; Save to map records it.
Small spectrometers have little signal and some stray light in the UV-B, so treat the UV index as approximate (about ±10–20 %). Recalibrate if you change the cosine corrector or fibre.

Recognises the technology of a lamp from its spectrum (low- or high-pressure sodium, mercury, metal halide, fluorescent, white LED, incandescent) and reports its colour temperature, blue share and melanopic ratio. In survey mode every recognised street light is mapped.

1. Point the input (ideally with a diffuser) at the lamp; shorten the integration time if it saturates.
2. Read the lamp type and the clues that led to it.
3. For a survey, set the interval and tap Survey ON, then walk or drive past the lights.
4. Open the Map: each lamp is a dot coloured by type.
Calibrate the response once in the Light tool (Use as lamp) for accurate colour temperature and blue share. Lamp types are recognised even without it.

Measures the faint red and far-red glow of chlorophyll (sun-induced fluorescence) by how much it fills in the oxygen absorption bands of sunlight at 687 and 760 nm. It reacts to plant stress (drought, heat, disease) earlier than NDVI does.

1. In direct sunlight, store a dark and a white reference on a white panel (Dark + white reference).\n2. Point the input at the leaves or canopy from the same direction.\n3. Read F760 and F687 as a percentage of the incoming light; Save to map to compare plants or plots.
Take a new white reference whenever the light changes (clouds, sun angle). Use it to compare plants measured the same way: at 1–2 nm resolution the absolute values are biased low.
Estimates nitrate from its UV absorption at 220 nm (corrected for organic matter with A275), and dissolved organic matter from UV254, with SUVA when you know the DOC.

1. Fill a 10 mm quartz cuvette with distilled water, put it in the holder and tap Dark + blank.
2. Rinse and fill the cuvette with the filtered water sample.
3. Read nitrate-N (and as nitrate), UV254 and, with DOC entered, SUVA.
4. For accurate nitrate, measure a standard (for example 5 mg/L N) and tap Calibrate.
Filter turbid samples (0.45 µm). Above about 10 mg/L N, dilute and multiply. Iron, bromide and some organics also absorb at 220 nm: compare with a lab result now and then.

Builds your own calibration with PLS regression: you teach it with samples whose values you know (sugar °Brix from a refractometer, dry matter from an oven, moisture…), then it predicts new samples from their spectrum alone.

1. Store a dark and a white reference (Dark + white reference).
2. Create a model: name, unit and wavelength range (for fruit and grain 700–1050 nm with an STS-NIR).
3. For each teaching sample: measure it, enter its reference value and tap Add sample. Use 20–50 samples covering the whole range.
4. Check the cross-validated error and Q²; then measure unknown samples and read the prediction.

Measure every sample the same way (probe, distance, light, temperature). Add samples from new batches or seasons over time. A Q² above 0.8 and an error well below the spread of your samples make a useful model.
Identifies materials from their Raman bands (laser light shifted by molecular vibrations): plastics, minerals, solvents and medicines, matched against a built-in and your own library.

1. Set up a 785 nm laser with a long-pass filter in front of the STS-NIR (a Raman probe does both). Wear laser eye protection.
2. Store a dark with the laser off.
3. Focus the laser on the sample and use long integration (1–10 s) with averaging.
4. Read the best match and its score; add your own reference samples to the library.
Fluorescent or dark samples swamp the weak Raman light. Black plastics burn: lower the power. If laser light leaks through the filter, use its measured position to fix the shift scale.
Measures the UV specific extinctions K232, K268 and ΔK of olive oil, as in EU Regulation 2568/91, and says whether they meet the extra virgin or virgin limits.

1. Dissolve 0.25 g of oil in 25 mL iso-octane.\n2. Fill a 10 mm quartz cuvette with iso-octane and tap Dark + blank.\n3. Fill the cuvette with the oil solution and read K232, K268, ΔK and the category.
Use a deuterium lamp and quartz (not glass or plastic) cuvettes. Dilute further if A232 exceeds about 1.5. UV indices are only part of the official grading.
Measures standard colour values: beer EBC and SRM (430 nm), wine colour intensity and hue (420, 520, 620 nm), and honey colour in mm Pfund with its grade.

1. Choose Beer, Wine or Honey.
2. Fill the cuvette with water (the blank) and tap Dark + blank.
3. Fill it with the prepared sample: degassed beer, wine in a 1 mm cell, or 50 % honey solution; enter path and dilution.
4. Read the values; Save to map records them.
Dark beers need dilution (enter it). Turbid beer reads too dark: filter it. Keep the cuvette the same way round for blank and sample.
Measures the temperature of glowing objects (kilns, furnaces, embers, molten metal, lamp filaments) from the shape of their thermal light, without knowing their emissivity.

1. Calibrate once: point at a halogen lamp of known colour temperature and tap Use as lamp.
2. Store a dark with the input covered.
3. Point at the glowing object; avoid saturation.
4. Read the temperature; narrow the wavelength range if the source has emission lines.
Works best from about 800 K (dull red glow) with the STS-NIR, and above 1200 K with visible units. Hot gases and flames with strong lines, or shiny surfaces reflecting other light, add error.
Measures the thickness of transparent films and coatings (lacquer, polymer foil, oxide on silicon, oil on water) from the interference fringes in their reflectance spectrum.

1. Store a dark and a white reference with the reflection probe on a white tile.
2. Place the probe on the film at the same distance.
3. Enter the film's refractive index and choose the substrate.
4. Read the thickness; the dashed model should follow the fringes.
Range about 0.5–50 µm with an STS. Thicker films show fringes too fine to resolve; very thin films need the substrate set correctly for the model fit.
Tests filters and eyewear in transmission: luminous transmittance and sunglass category, UV400 and blue-light blocking, cut-on wavelength of colour filters and optical density of laser goggles.

1. Put the lamp and spectrometer across the holder with nothing in between; store a dark and the open beam.\n2. Put the lens or filter in the beam, square to it.\n3. Read the category, UV, blue and cut-on values, and the optical density at the wavelength you set.
UV checks need a UV unit and a lamp with UV (deuterium). Optical density above about 2–3 is beyond the dynamic range: the app then shows a lower bound.
Checks the spectrometer itself: dark level and read noise, hot pixels, linearity against integration time and wavelength accuracy against a mercury-argon lamp, and writes a dated report.

1. Dark test: cover the input (or let the shutter close) and tap Run dark test.
2. Linearity: point at a steady lamp at about half scale and tap Run linearity test.
3. Wavelength: point at a mercury-argon lamp and tap Check wavelength.
4. Share the report for your records or for support.
Run it when the unit is new and every few months. Rising noise, new hot pixels or a wavelength shift above 0.5 nm are reasons to recalibrate or service the unit.
The lamp saturates the detector: shorten the integration time before calibrating.
Scan a QR code or barcode

With a web address set, every new confirmed fire is sent there as a short JSON message (time, position, confidence, flame temperature, spectrometer), so a phone left watching a valley can raise the alarm elsewhere: your server, a chat or automation webhook. Keep the phone on mains power with the screen kept on.
Total ozone and nitrogen dioxide columns from the direct sun, like a Dobson / Pandora instrument.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV) for ozone or a visible unit for NO₂, a collimator with ND filter pointed at the sun, and a calibration.
SPAD-like chlorophyll index of a leaf from light through it at 650 nm and in the near infrared.
Needs: a leaf clip or cuvette holder with a light source, red and near-infrared range (645–785 nm).
PPFD, daily light integral, colour shares and the red : far-red ratio of grow lights and daylight.
Needs: the visible range, the Light tool calibration (lamp response and scale) and a cosine corrector.
Forel-Ule colour index of lakes and the sea, with chlorophyll and cyanobacteria hints.
Needs: 400–710 nm, a white panel reference in the same daylight, and a view of the water surface.
Munsell soil-chart notation of a soil sample from its reflectance, as used in soil surveys.
Needs: the visible range (380–780 nm), a reflection probe with a lamp and a white reference.
Reads colour test kits for chlorine, phosphate, ammonia, nitrite and iron, or your own method.
Needs: a cuvette holder with a light source and a blank with the reagent but no sample.
pH of a sample from the colour of an indicator dye, read at two wavelengths.
Needs: 430–620 nm, a cuvette holder, an indicator dye and a blank.
Fluorescence of chlorophyll, phycocyanin, fluorescein, quinine, oil and UV security marks.
Needs: an LED at the right excitation wavelength, a cuvette at 90° (or a probe with a filter), and a blank.
Concentration and purity (A260/A280, A260/A230) of DNA, RNA and protein in a quartz cuvette.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV, 228–322 nm), a deuterium or xenon lamp, a quartz cuvette and a buffer blank.
Optical density at 600 nm over time, with growth rate, doubling time and lag of a culture.
Needs: 595–605 nm, a cuvette holder with a light source and a blank with growth medium.
Colour rendering index Ra, R9 and the TM-30 fidelity and gamut indices of a lamp.
Needs: the visible range (380–780 nm) and the lamp-response calibration from the Light tool.
Colour gamut, primaries and white point of a phone, monitor or TV screen.
Needs: the visible range (380–780 nm); the probe held against the screen.
Suggests historical pigments (ultramarine, vermilion, ochres…) from reflectance features, as in FORS.
Needs: 420–700 nm (better to 1000 nm), a reflection probe with a halogen lamp and a white reference.
Absorption and fluorescence lines of gemstones: ruby, sapphire, emerald, garnet, zircon and imitations.
Needs: a light through the stone (absorption) or a UV or blue LED (fluorescence); the visible range.
Personal melanopic light exposure through the day against the daytime, evening and night recommendations.
Needs: the visible range, the Light tool calibration, and the probe worn facing forward at eye level.
Personal erythemal UV dose in standard erythema doses (SED) with time to the typical sunburn dose.
Needs: a UV unit (STS-UV, 290–400 nm), a cosine corrector and the UV index scale.
Erythema (redness), melanin and carotenoid indices of skin from its reflectance, for research and wellness.
Needs: 555–660 nm (440 nm for carotenoids), a reflection probe with a lamp and a white reference.
Pulse rate, perfusion index and RMSSD from light through a fingertip (photoplethysmography).
Needs: red or near-infrared range, a light source shining through the fingertip into the probe, short exposures.
Daily exposure and physiology logs with a participant code: share or upload them for a study.
Needs: logs from the light, UV, skin, pulse or greenhouse tools.
Identifies gas discharge tubes, measures the Rydberg constant and Planck’s constant with LEDs.
Needs: discharge tubes (hydrogen, helium, neon…), or LEDs with a voltmeter and an adjustable supply.

Measures the total ozone column (Dobson units) from the ratio of direct sunlight at 310 and 330 nm, and nitrogen dioxide by differential optical absorption (DOAS) between 425 and 490 nm. Experimental: the results depend on careful calibration and pointing.

1. Fit a collimator and a neutral-density filter, point at the sun and store a dark. 2. Ozone: calibrate once, either with a known ozone value (satellite or a nearby station) or with a Langley series on a clear morning. 3. NO₂: import an NO₂ cross-section file (wavelength, cm²/molecule), store a reference spectrum near noon on a clean day, then measure. 4. Save results with the position.
Only clear sky around the sun gives usable data. Ozone needs the STS-UV; NO₂ a visible unit. The NO₂ column shown is relative to the reference spectrum unless the reference was taken in clean air.

Measures leaf chlorophyll the way a SPAD meter does: transmittance in the red chlorophyll band (650 nm) against the near infrared (940 or 780 nm). The default scale gives SPAD-like values and an approximate chlorophyll content.

1. Store a dark, then a reference with the clip empty. 2. Clamp a leaf between the veins. 3. Read the index; average 3–5 leaves per plant. 4. For SPAD-equal values, measure one leaf with a SPAD meter and enter its value to calibrate.
Avoid veins and wet leaves. Low values (below about 30 in cereals) point to nitrogen shortage.

Turns a calibrated light measurement into plant terms: PPFD (µmol/m²/s), the daily light integral, the shares of blue, green, red and far-red photons, and the red : far-red ratio that controls stretching and flowering.

1. Calibrate in the Light tool (lamp response and a lux or PPFD scale), and prepare the darks for auto-exposure. 2. Point the cosine corrector up at plant height. 3. Read PPFD and R:FR; start the logger to add up the daily light integral.
Typical DLI targets: lettuce 12–17, tomatoes 20–30 mol/m²/day. R:FR above 1 is open daylight; below 0.5 is deep shade.

Gives the Forel-Ule colour of water (1 = deep blue sea to 21 = brown humic lake), the scale used since 1890 and by ocean-colour satellites, plus hints for chlorophyll (R705/R665) and the cyanobacteria pigment phycocyanin (dip near 620 nm).

1. In steady daylight, store a dark and then a white-panel reference. 2. Point the probe at the water at about 40° from vertical, away from the sun, avoiding sun glint and foam. 3. Read the FU index; save it with the position.
Use a longer integration for the water than for the panel: the tool corrects for it. Cloud changes between panel and water spoil the result.

Matches a soil\'s colour to the nearest Munsell soil-chart chip (for example 10YR 4/3), the notation used in soil descriptions. Darker values often mean more organic matter, redder hues more iron oxides, grey or bluish hues waterlogging.
1. Store a dark and a white reference. 2. Measure a flat, crumbled sample, dry and moist if needed. 3. Read the notation and the nearest chips with their colour difference.
Moisture darkens soil by one or two value steps: record the state. The match uses D65 daylight and the 2° observer.

Reads colour test kits with a spectrometer instead of the eye: DPD chlorine, molybdenum-blue phosphate, indophenol ammonia, Griess nitrite and phenanthroline iron, or a custom method at a wavelength you choose.

1. Prepare a blank with the reagent in clean water, store a dark and the blank. 2. Add the reagent to the sample, wait the kit\'s reaction time and measure. 3. For best accuracy, calibrate with a standard of known concentration.
The built-in responses are typical values: the kit\'s own calibration is better. Above the range shown, dilute and measure again.
Measures pH from the ratio of an indicator dye\'s two coloured forms, which is far more precise than reading a colour by eye. Each dye covers about pKa ± 1.
1. Choose the dye. Store a dark and a blank of the sample without dye. 2. Add the dye and measure. 3. For best accuracy, store the fully acid and fully basic forms of the dye once.
Use the same dye concentration each time. Temperature and salt shift pKa slightly: calibrate in conditions like your samples.

A simple fluorimeter: an LED excites the sample and the spectrometer reads the emission window. Presets for chlorophyll-a, phycocyanin (cyanobacteria), fluorescein (leak and dye tracing), quinine, oil in water and UV security marks.
1. Place the LED at 90° to the probe, cuvette in between. Store a dark and a blank (clean water) with the LED on. 2. Measure the sample. 3. Calibrate with one standard of known concentration.
Keep the LED, cuvette and integration time the same between blank, standard and samples. Very strong samples quench: dilute them.
UV absorbance of DNA, RNA and protein: concentration from A260 (or A280 for protein) and purity from the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios, with background correction at 320 nm.

1. Use a quartz cuvette and a deuterium or xenon lamp. Store a dark and a buffer blank. 2. Measure the sample, set the path and dilution. 3. Pure DNA gives 260/280 about 1.8 and 260/230 about 2.0–2.2.
Low 260/280 points to protein or phenol; low 260/230 to salts such as guanidine. Keep A260 between 0.1 and 1 for good accuracy.
Follows a bacterial or yeast culture by optical density at 600 nm and fits the exponential phase: specific growth rate, doubling time, lag time and the maximum density.
1. Store a dark and a blank with sterile medium. 2. Put the culture in the cuvette and start recording; set the interval. 3. The fit appears once the exponential phase is clear.
OD600 above about 1 is no longer linear: dilute the sample and enter the dilution. OD depends on the instrument, so compare cultures on the same set-up.

Calculates the CIE colour rendering index (Ra, and R1–R14 including the deep-red R9) and the IES TM-30 fidelity (Rf) and gamut (Rg) indices, with the colour temperature and Duv, from the calibrated spectrum of a lamp.
1. Calibrate the detector response once with a lamp of known temperature (Light tool). 2. Store a dark and point at the lamp, without saturating. 3. Read Ra, R9, Rf and Rg; save the result.
Ra above 90 and R9 above 50 are good for homes, shops and photography. Without the response calibration the results are wrong.
Measures a screen\'s colour: the chromaticity of its red, green and blue primaries and white, the gamut area and its coverage of sRGB, DCI-P3 and Rec.2020, and the white point colour temperature.

1. Store a dark. Show a full-screen white, red, green and blue patch in turn (Show patches on this phone does it for this phone). 2. Hold the probe against the screen and store each patch. 3. Read the gamut figures.
Turn off night mode and auto-brightness. OLED screens usually cover more of DCI-P3 than LCDs.

Fibre-optic reflectance spectroscopy (FORS) of paintings and manuscripts: the tool finds inflection points, absorption minima and maxima in the reflectance and suggests matching historical pigments, without touching the object.
1. Store a dark and a white reference (a diffuse white standard). 2. Hold the probe at a fixed distance over a single-colour area. 3. Read the suggestions with their score.
Suggestions are a guide, not proof: mixtures and binders change spectra. Confirm with Raman or XRF. Keep lamp light short to protect the object.

Shows the absorption lines of gemstones in transmitted light (as a hand spectroscope does) and the fluorescence of chromium in ruby and spinel, and compares them with diagnostic lines of common gems and imitations.

1. Absorption: store a dark, then an open-beam reference, put the stone in the beam and measure. 2. Fluorescence: shine a blue or UV LED on the stone and measure with the dark only. 3. Read the suggestions.
A match narrows the options; it does not certify a gem. Treated and synthetic stones can show the same lines.

Logs the melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melanopic EDI) that reaches the eye through the day and compares it with the 2022 expert recommendations: at least 250 lx during the day, at most 10 lx in the last three hours before sleep and at most 1 lx during sleep. For wellness and research, not a medical device.

1. Calibrate in the Light tool and prepare the darks (auto-exposure steps). 2. Wear the probe facing forward near eye level. 3. Start the logger; set your usual wake and bed times. 4. Review the day\'s summary or export it in the Exposure diary.
Exposure depends on where you look: keep the probe at eye level. Logging keeps running while other tabs are open; keep the phone charged.

Adds up personal erythemal UV exposure in standard erythema doses (1 SED = 100 J/m²) and shows the time left to the typical sunburn dose for a chosen skin type. For awareness and research, not a medical device.
1. Set the UV index scale once in the UV index tool. 2. Choose a skin type. 3. Start the logger and keep the cosine corrector facing the sky.
Sunburn doses vary widely between people: the time shown is a rough guide, not a safe limit. Use shade, clothing and sunscreen.

Measures skin colour indices from reflectance: the erythema index (redness, from 560 and 650 nm), the melanin index and a relative carotenoid index, with change from your baseline. For cosmetic, wellness and research use; it does not diagnose any condition.

1. Store a dark and a white reference with the probe at the same distance. 2. Hold the probe lightly on the skin, without pressing. 3. Set a baseline, then follow changes (for example after sun exposure); log readings with a site label.
Pressure squeezes blood out and lowers the erythema index. Measure the same site under the same conditions.

Estimates pulse rate, perfusion index and the beat-to-beat variability RMSSD from light passing through a fingertip, like a fitness tracker. It does not measure oxygen saturation and is not a medical device.

1. Shine a lamp or LED through the fingertip into the probe; store a dark. 2. Tap Fast exposures (20 ms) and keep the finger still for 15 seconds. 3. Read the values once the quality is above 60 %; record if you need a log.
Movement and cold fingers spoil the signal. Do not use it to make decisions about your health; see a doctor for any concern.

Collects the daily logs of the light dose, UV dose, skin, pulse and greenhouse tools, labelled with a participant code, for sharing with a study team or uploading to the study server. Data stay on the phone until you share them.

1. Enter the participant code given by the study (or scan it). 2. Pick a day and share the zip, or enter the study\'s https upload address and upload. 3. Follow the study\'s information sheet and consent form.
Research use needs informed consent and ethics approval by the study team. The export contains no name: only the code, times and measurements.

A school and university lab: identifies the gas in discharge tubes from its lines, measures the Rydberg constant from the hydrogen Balmer lines, and Planck\'s constant from LEDs\' wavelength and turn-on voltage.

1. Store a dark and point at a discharge tube. 2. For Rydberg, use a hydrogen tube: the Balmer lines give R. 3. For Planck, for each LED find the voltage where it just starts to glow, enter it and add the LED; two or more LEDs give h.
Discharge tubes run at high voltage: use proper holders. LED turn-on voltages are read more reliably from the current–voltage curve.
Store a dark and a blank (reagent in clean water) to read the kit.
Above the method\'s range (%1$s): dilute the sample and measure again.
Calibrate with a standard: enter its concentration and tap Calibrate while it is in the cuvette.
DPD turns pink with free chlorine, read at 515 nm. Read within one minute of adding the reagent.
Molybdenum blue, read at 880 nm (710 nm on visible units). Wait the kit\'s reaction time, usually 2–10 minutes.
Indophenol (salicylate) blue-green, read at 655 nm, after about 15 minutes.
Griess reagent turns pink-violet, read at 540 nm after 10 minutes.
Phenanthroline orange-red, read at 510 nm after 3 minutes.
Choose the wavelength of your method\'s colour and calibrate with a standard.
Store a dark and a blank of the sample without dye to read the pH.
Outside the dye\'s useful range (pH %1$s–%2$s): choose another dye.
For best accuracy, measure the dye fully acid (pH well below pKa) and fully basic (well above) once.
Use the same amount of dye in every sample; the blank is the sample itself without dye.
Store a dark and a blank (clean water with the LED on) to measure fluorescence.
Calibrate with a standard of known concentration; the signal is proportional below about 100 µg/L.
Blue LED (450 nm), emission 670–700 nm: algae in water.
Orange LED (590 nm), emission 640–665 nm: cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).
Blue LED (470 nm), emission 505–540 nm: leak and groundwater tracing.
UV LED (365 nm), emission 425–475 nm: tonic water, the classic teaching standard.
UV LED (365 nm), emission 400–500 nm: aromatic oil in water (relative).
UV LED (365 nm): shows the emission of banknote and document security marks.
Store a dark and a buffer blank in the quartz cuvette.
Pure DNA: 260/280 ≈ 1.8, RNA ≈ 2.0; 260/230 should be 2.0–2.2. Protein uses A280 = 1 for 1 mg/mL.
Store a dark and a blank with sterile medium to read OD600.
OD above 1: dilute the sample for a linear reading.
Time in hours; the green band is the fitted exponential phase.
Readings are taken at the interval while recording, also from other tabs.
The simulated culture grows 60 times faster than real time.
Lines are compared with NIST wavelengths of common discharge tubes.
Point at a hydrogen tube: R comes from the Balmer lines (n = 3, 4, 5, 6 to 2), converted to vacuum wavelengths.
For each LED: point it at the probe, find the voltage at which it just starts to glow, enter it and add the LED.
Store a dark and a white-panel reference in the same daylight first.
FU 1–5 blue open water, 6–13 green waters with algae, 14–21 brown waters with humic matter or sediment.
Store a dark and a reference with the clip empty first.
To read SPAD units exactly, measure one leaf with a SPAD meter and enter its value.
The response and the scale come from the Light tool. Prepare darks lets the logger change the exposure from 2 ms to 2 s automatically, from moonlight to sunlight.
This unit has no shutter: cover the input while the darks are taken.
Simulator: calibrates on the simulated lamp, then takes the scale from a simulated lux meter.
Simulator: calibrates on the simulated lamp, then takes the scale from a simulated quantum (PPFD) meter.
PPFD needs the Light tool calibration (lamp response and scale).
R:FR is the photon ratio 655–665 / 725–735 nm: daylight about 1.1–1.2, shade below 0.5.
The logger adds PPFD over time while it runs, also from other tabs; Reset starts a new day.
Experimental: column results need a careful calibration and clear sky around the sun.
Calibrate once: with a known ozone value from a satellite or a station, or with a Langley series on a clear morning (air mass 2–6).
Import an NO₂ absorption cross-section file (two columns: wavelength in nm, cm²/molecule) to measure NO₂.
Store a reference spectrum near noon on a clean day; later spectra give the NO₂ column relative to it.
Treats the reference as free of NO₂, so the full column is shown.
Store a dark and a white reference first.
All Munsell colours (not only soil pages)
ΔE00 below about 2 is a close match. Record whether the sample was dry or moist.
Neutral grey: often waterlogged (gleyed) or very low in iron.
Dark: usually rich in organic matter.
Red: well drained, rich in iron oxides (haematite).
Brown or yellowish brown: iron oxides (goethite) and organic matter.
Calibrate the detector response with a lamp of known temperature first: without it the indices are wrong.
Signal too weak or no dark: point at the lamp and store a dark.
Ra above 90 and R9 above 50 render colours well. Rg above 100 means more saturated colours than the reference.
The lamp-response calibration is shared with the Light tool.
Show each patch full screen, hold the probe against the screen and store it.
Hold the probe on the screen. Tap to store this colour and show the next one.
Coverage is the share of each standard\'s triangle (in u′v′) inside the screen\'s triangle.
Store a dark and a white reference first.
A suggestion, not an identification: confirm with other methods. Keep the lamp on the object briefly.
Store a dark and an open-beam reference (no stone) first.
Put the stone in the light beam; turn it to find the strongest lines.
Shine a blue or UV LED on the stone; chromium gives sharp red lines near 694 nm (ruby) or 685 nm (spinel).
A guide only: treated and synthetic stones can show the same lines as natural ones.

The exposure tools (light dose, UV dose, skin indices, pulse and the exposure diary) are for general wellness, education and research. PocketSpectro is not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any medical condition. The values are estimates that depend on calibration and use. Do not use them to make decisions about your health; consult a doctor or other healthcare professional for any medical question.
When used in a research study, follow the study\'s information sheet and consent form. Measurements stay on this phone until you share or upload them.
Wellness and research use only. Not a medical device.
Melanopic EDI needs the Light tool calibration (lamp response and lux scale).
Daytime: aim for at least 250 lx melanopic EDI.
Evening (3 h before bed): at most 10 lx.
Today: hour of day against melanopic EDI (log scale); the line is 250 lx.
Recommendations: Brown et al. (2022), PLOS Biology. Values are at the eye, so wear the probe facing forward at eye level.
Changes the integration time to keep the signal in range (needs prepared darks).
Logs go to the Exposure diary, one file per day; logging continues on other tabs.
A simulated day (home, commute, office, evening) running 120 times faster. Start at:
Set the UV index scale in the UV index tool first.
Time to the typical sunburn dose
Type I: always burns, never tans.
Type II: usually burns, tans with difficulty.
Type III: sometimes burns, tans gradually.
Type IV: rarely burns, tans easily.
Type V: very rarely burns, tans very easily.
Type VI: deeply pigmented, almost never burns.
1 SED = 100 J/m² erythemal. The sunburn doses are typical values; individual sensitivity varies widely, so this is not a safe-exposure limit.
The simulated sun runs 60 times faster. Use the simulated UV meter to set the scale.
Set the scale from the simulated UV meter
Store a dark and a white reference first, with the probe at the same distance.
Indices after Diffey et al. (1984). Touch lightly: pressure lowers the erythema index.
Keep the finger still and warm. Does not measure blood oxygen. Not for medical use.
Use for research only with informed consent and the study\'s ethics approval. The export holds the code, times and measurements, no name.
No logs yet: start a logger in the light dose, UV dose, pulse or greenhouse tool, or log a skin reading.
The zip holds one CSV per log with UTC and epoch times, and a README with the code, app version and instrument.
Checks food against fraud: olive oil grade (UV K232/K268), beer, wine and honey colour, sugar and dry matter by NIR prediction, and spectral fingerprints of genuine products to spot substitutes.
Sorts plastics for recycling: NIR fingerprints of PE, PP, PET, PS and PVC with the spectral match, a trained model for your own waste stream, and Raman for dark or thin items.
Screens tablets against falsified medicines: Raman and NIR fingerprints compared with genuine packs, the UV security marks on packaging, and the dissolved active ingredient by absorbance.

A phone left watching a valley: fire detection with alerts to a server, flame temperature, smoke from the sun photometer\'s aerosol optical depth and NO₂, and vegetation dryness before the fire season.

Personal exposure and wellness logging for research: melanopic light dose against the 2022 recommendations, UV dose, skin indices, pulse and the lamps around the participant, exported per day with a participant code. Non-medical.
Crop and soil checks in the field: NDVI and red edge, leaf chlorophyll, sun-induced fluorescence, greenhouse lighting (PPFD, DLI, R:FR) and soil colour.
Drinking, river and lake water: UV254 and nitrate, the Forel-Ule colour and algae hints, colour test kits, pH and fluorescence of algae and tracers.
Non-contact study of paintings and manuscripts: pigment suggestions by FORS, colour measurement for conservation records, Raman and varnish thickness.
Classic experiments: discharge tubes and the Rydberg and Planck constants, the Beer–Lambert law, reaction kinetics, pH with indicators, bacterial growth and the colour of light.
